report:
## Conclusion

The evidence on hypnosis (hypnotherapy) for smoking cessation is **inconclusive and generally unimpressive**. The most authoritative synthesis, the **Cochrane systematic review** (Barnes et al., updated through 2019), found no consistent evidence that hypnotherapy has a greater effect on six-month quit rates than other interventions (e.g., counseling) or no treatment; trials were small, heterogeneous, and often of low quality, and pooled effect sizes did not reach statistical significance (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20927723/). The UK's **NICE** rapid evidence review similarly concluded there is no strong evidence hypnotherapy improves long-term abstinence, citing the same underlying systematic review base (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209/evidence/ph10-rapid-review-of-nonnhs-treatments-for-smoking-cessation-pdf-392073181532).

More recent, broader analyses complicate this picture somewhat. A 2023 meta-analytic review in *Frontiers in Psychology* found that across five reviews (including three Cochrane analyses), effect sizes for hypnosis versus control ranged widely (d = 0.12–0.84), with only two of six reported effects reaching statistical significance—suggesting modest, inconsistent benefit (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1330238/full). A newer 2025 review (Ekanayake & Elkins), which took a wider-lens approach across 63 studies since 1968, reported more favorable overall support for hypnosis, though this contrasts with Cochrane's stricter RCT-only methodology (https://www.ishhypnosis.org/encyclopedia/the-potential-benefit-of-hypnosis-for-smoking-cessation/).

**Bottom line:** Hypnosis may help some individuals quit smoking, and it is generally safe, but rigorous trial evidence does not clearly show it outperforms other cessation methods (nicotine replacement, counseling, medications) or placebo. It should not be considered a first-line, evidence-based treatment; approaches with stronger backing (varenicline, bupropion, NRT, behavioral counseling) remain the recommended standard, though hypnosis could be tried as an adjunct for motivated individuals.
